title: Which fit questions do consultancies ask most, and what are they testing?
description: The fit questions you are most likely to be asked in a consulting interview, what each one is really testing, and how to answer.
hook: Most consulting fit interviews come back to eight questions: tell me about yourself, why consulting and why this firm, and stories about leadership, failure, persuasion, impact, initiative and a weakness. Each one tests a quality you would need on a client team, so the best preparation is a small set of true stories, not a script for every question. Here is what each question is really asking and how to show it.
body:
The eight questions at a glance

QuestionWhat they are testingWhat to show
Tell me about yourselfCan you explain yourself clearly and briefly?A thread through your choices, two proof points, why now

A time you led through difficultyWill people follow you when it is hard?The decision you made and how you brought people with you
A time you failedHonesty and ability to learnClear ownership and a changed habit
Persuading without authorityInfluence with clients and senior peopleThat you understood the other person's position
Your biggest achievementDo things change because of you?A measured result and your personal part in it
A time you took initiativeDo you start things nobody asked for?What you noticed, what you did, what changed
Your biggest weaknessSelf-awarenessA real weakness and the habit you use to manage it

What each question is really asking

Tell me about yourself

This is your story in 60 to 90 seconds, not your CV read aloud. Give where you started and what drove your choices, two moments you are proud of, and why consulting makes sense now. The "Tell me about yourself" breakdown shows a weak and a strong version side by side.

Why consulting? Why this firm?

The interviewer wants proof of real homework. Tie your motivation to something you have actually done, then add a reason for this firm that you could not have copied from its website: a conversation with someone there, a practice area, the way it staffs projects. "I want to solve interesting problems" could describe any career. See strong and weak "Why consulting?" answers.

Leadership through difficulty

They are asking whether people follow you when things go wrong. Be specific about what you did: the conversation you had, the decision you made, the trade-off you accepted.

Failure

Choose a real failure that mattered, not a disguised strength. Own your part without blaming others, and spend most of your time on what you now do differently. The failure question guide shows how to keep it honest without hurting your chances.

Persuasion without authority

The detail interviewers listen for is whether you understood why the other person disagreed, and how you used that: data, a small test, or finding a measure you both cared about.

Biggest achievement

Pick the result where you made the clearest difference and put a number on it if you can. "We" is fine for the team, but say what you personally did that would not have happened without you.

Initiative

A good initiative story starts with something you noticed, a problem or an opportunity, then what you did about it without waiting for permission, and what changed.

Weakness

Choose a real weakness that would not stop you doing the job, show how it has shown up, and spend most of the answer on how you manage it. "I'm a perfectionist" sounds rehearsed. "I used to take on too much myself; now I agree priorities with my manager at the start of each week" sounds honest. More in the weakness answer guide.

How the big firms frame it

The questions are similar everywhere, but the format differs. McKinsey calls its version the Personal Experience Interview. As of 2026, its interviewing page asks you to prepare two examples for each area it assesses, which include personal impact, entrepreneurial drive and inclusive leadership, and says the interview should be a conversation rather than a rehearsed story. Expect to stay on one story while the interviewer probes for detail. The McKinsey interview process guide covers the full format.

BCG's interview process page describes a values-driven firm and lists integrity, intellectual curiosity, creative thinking, a collaborative mindset and drive as what it looks for. Formats vary by office and role, so ask your recruiter what to expect.

One set of stories covers most questions

You do not need a separate story for each question. Six to eight well-prepared stories will cover almost anything. For each one, write four factual anchors: the problem, your own decision, what changed and what you learned. Then note the pressure point an interviewer might push on, such as a colleague who disagreed with you in a leadership story, or a trade-off you misjudged in a failure story.

A single story often answers several questions. A project where you rescued a late deadline might work for leadership, impact and persuasion, as long as you tell a different part of it each time. Stories can come from studies, community work or personal commitments, as long as the details are concrete.

Expect the follow-ups

Interviewers interrupt with questions like:

What did you actually say to her?
Why did you choose that option and not the other one?

Your story should survive being taken apart. If you cannot answer the third "why", choose a smaller story you know in detail.

Common mistakes

  • One story per question, all memorised. You end up reciting. Prepare fewer stories and know them deeply.
  • Everything is "we". The interviewer is hiring you. Say "I" for the actions you took.
  • No result. End with what changed and what you learned.

Practise: which quality is this testing?

Name the quality and the story you would use before you open each answer.

1. "Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone more senior than you."

Show the answer

Persuasion without authority, and at McKinsey, personal impact. Use a story where you understood their view, changed their mind with evidence or a small test, and kept the relationship intact.

2. "Describe a time you worked with people very different from you."

Show the answer

Teamwork and inclusive leadership. Show what you did to bring out the best in people with different views or backgrounds, not just that the team got along.

3. "Tell me about something you started that nobody asked you to do."

Show the answer

Initiative, often called entrepreneurial drive. Start with what you noticed, then the step you took without permission, then the result.

Where to practise next

Build your story bank with the fit interview guide, then work through each question's own article. Say every story out loud before the real thing.
outro: Build and save your stories in the free fit stories builder. Next in this topic: How do you come across as clear and calm in a case interview?
